Arithmetic & Geometric Sequences: Rules and Notation

Traci BaekSeptember 30, 2026
HSF-BF.A.2 — Arithmetic and geometric sequences: explicit and recursive rules.
Two questions to ask: Do I add the same amount each time, or multiply by the same factor? Then check where the term numbering starts.
1 · Different notation, same term
NotationRead it as
\(a_n\) or \(a(n)\)The term at position \(n\)
\(a_1\) or \(a(1)\)The first term when numbering starts at 1
\(a_{n-1}\)The term immediately before \(a_n\)
\(a_{n+1}\)The term immediately after \(a_n\)

The letter can change: \(a_n\), \(g(n)\), and \(c_n\) all name sequence terms. However, \(a_{n+1}\) means “the next term”; it does not mean \(a_n+1\).

2 · Arithmetic: add a fixed difference

For \(2,5,8,11,\ldots\), subtract consecutive terms: \(5-2=8-5=11-8=3\). The common difference is \(d=3\).

RuleGeneral form (starts at 1)
Explicit: go directly to a term\(a_n=a_1+d(n-1)\), integers \(n\ge1\)
Recursive: use the previous termStarting value \(a_1\); \(a_n=a_{n-1}+d\), integers \(n\ge2\)
Recursive: use next-term notationStarting value \(a_1\); \(a_{n+1}=a_n+d\), integers \(n\ge1\)
Solved example · 1, 5, 9, 13, …

Difference: \(d=4\). Explicit: \(a_n=1+4(n-1)=4n-3\).

Fifth term: \(a_5=1+4(5-1)=17\).

100th term: \(a_{100}=1+4(100-1)=397\).

Recursive: \(a_1=1\), \(a_{n+1}=a_n+4\) for integers \(n\ge1\).

Function notation says the same thing: \(a(n)=4n-3\), so \(a(5)=17\).

Solved example · A decreasing sequence

\(11,8,5,2,\ldots\) has \(d=-3\).

\(a_n=11+(-3)(n-1)=14-3n\). Thus \(a_5=14-15=-1\).

Recursive: \(a_1=11\), \(a_{n+1}=a_n-3\) for integers \(n\ge1\).

3 · Geometric: multiply by a fixed ratio

For \(3,6,12,24,\ldots\), divide consecutive terms: \(6/3=12/6=24/12=2\). The common ratio is \(r=2\).

RuleGeneral form (starts at 1)
Explicit\(a_n=a_1r^{n-1}\), integers \(n\ge1\)
Recursive, previous termStarting value \(a_1\); \(a_n=r a_{n-1}\), integers \(n\ge2\)
Recursive, next termStarting value \(a_1\); \(a_{n+1}=r a_n\), integers \(n\ge1\)
Solved example · 3, 6, 12, 24, …

\(a_1=3\), \(r=2\). Explicit: \(a_n=3\cdot2^{n-1}\).

\(a_5=3\cdot2^4=48\). Recursive: \(a_1=3\), \(a_{n+1}=2a_n\) for integers \(n\ge1\).

The exponent is 4 because reaching term 5 takes four multiplications after term 1.

Solved example · Fractions and negative ratios

\(16,8,4,2,\ldots\): \(r=1/2\), so \(a_n=16(1/2)^{n-1}\) and \(a_5=1\).

\(2,-6,18,-54,\ldots\): \(r=-3\), so \(a_n=2(-3)^{n-1}\). Parentheses keep the negative ratio together; signs alternate.

4 · When the first index is 0
ArithmeticGeometric
\(a_n=a_0+dn\)\(a_n=a_0r^n\)
Solved example · p(0) = −2, then multiply by 5

\(p(1)=5(-2)=-10\), \(p(2)=5(-10)=-50\).

Explicit: \(p(n)=-2\cdot5^n\) for integers \(n\ge0\).

Recursive: \(p(0)=-2\), \(p(n)=5p(n-1)\) for integers \(n\ge1\).

5 · See the difference

Blue blocks: add 2 each time. Teal blocks: multiply by 2 each time.

ArithmeticGeometric
2 → 4 → 6 → 8
+2 each time
\(a_n=2+2(n-1)=2n\)		2 → 4 → 8 → 16
×2 each time
\(a_n=2\cdot2^{n-1}\)
\(a_1=2,\ a_{n+1}=a_n+2\)\(a_1=2,\ a_{n+1}=2a_n\)

For both recursive rules, \(n\) is an integer with \(n\ge1\). For both explicit rules, \(n\ge1\).

Quick check: Find the first index. Compare differences or ratios. Write the starting value. Then test your rule on two given terms.
